title: Should my freelance editor use AI, or should our marketing team buy the tool?
summary: Decide who should own AI footage preparation when a marketing team works with a freelance editor, based on access, recurring work, and the handoff.
body_markdown:
## What you’ll take away


- Assign a recurring task before assigning a subscription.
- Agree on the handoff with the editor before preparing a large amount of material.
- Separate tool ownership from responsibility for the final story.


## Start with the task that creates the delay


Ask where work waits today. The editor may be searching hours of interviews for a claim marketing already knows it needs. Marketing may be waiting for a transcript before it can write the brief. Or the footage may arrive without a clear story, leaving the editor to resolve a messaging decision.


Only the first two are straightforward preparation opportunities. An AI subscription will not decide a campaign's audience or reconcile stakeholder priorities. Name the missing deliverable: timecoded candidate quotes, an interview stringout, supporting shots, or a source-based sequence.


## When the editor should own the workflow


The freelancer is a natural owner when they receive the complete source package, understand its structure, and will maintain the Premiere project. They can incorporate an assistant into the preparation process without asking marketing to become a second editor.


Discuss the desired deliverable and review expectations rather than prescribing unverified time savings. Ask how source selections, revisions, and final project files will be handed over. Whether the freelancer uses an assistant is part of their working method; the client still needs a clear agreement about what it receives.


## When marketing can own useful preparation


Marketing can help when it knows the buyer questions and regularly revisits the interview archive. A producer can find candidate answers and explain why they matter before the editor begins assembly. The useful output is a source-linked brief, not an unchangeable finished video.


In Wideframe, point a chat at the authorized interview folder and use the[transcript workflow](https://try.wideframe.com/skills/export-transcript/) or topic-based selections. Start with one real request, such as finding implementation answers for an upcoming sales campaign. Share the selected sources and intent with the freelancer, leaving room for better editorial choices.


## Agree on a handoff the editor wants


Before preparing the whole shoot, ask whether the editor prefers timecoded notes, a selects sequence, or a project organized in a particular way. The same information can be useful in one format and inconvenient in another. An editor who needs source handles should not receive only tightly cropped exports.


A practical handoff includes the question each selection answers and access to the longer source. Mark must-use material separately from optional candidates. Do not overwhelm the editor with every remotely relevant passage or impose a narrative order that no one has reviewed.


## Keep costs and access explicit


Decide who pays for the tool, which source material can be processed, and who retains the reusable work after the engagement. These are operational choices for the relationship, not details to leave implicit. Check the vendor's current account and team arrangements rather than assuming one login should be shared.


Wideframe's[pricing page](https://try.wideframe.com/pricing/) offers individual and team discussions; choose the arrangement appropriate to the actual users. Do not infer shared workspaces or collaborative editing features from the existence of team pricing. Specify how files and projects will move using your established process.


## Avoid doing the same edit twice


If marketing makes a detailed assembly and the freelancer rebuilds it from scratch, find out why. Perhaps the handoff lacks sources, the story brief changed, or the preparation was too prescriptive. Fix that division of work rather than adding another layer of instructions.


Keep one person responsible for the master sequence. Marketing can own audience and claim priorities, while the editor owns the craft and technical finish. An assistant can help either person prepare material, but it should not blur who resolves an editorial disagreement.


## Choose based on next month's work too


For a single one-off project, the freelancer's existing setup may be sufficient. For recurring interviews and campaign requests, an internal preparation capability may be valuable even when finishing remains external. The important question is who will use the workflow again with enough context to make it useful.


Begin with a small, agreed handoff and expand the recurring task as the collaboration settles. The result should be less repeated explanation and better source material for the editor, not a new software responsibility with no owner.
